Sound engineering technicians set up and operate sound equipment to record, synchronize, mix, edit or reproduce music, voices and sound effects for stage, film, television, podcast and sports productions. They deliver sound files, recording logs and equipment anomaly records; whether the position leans towards live or post-production work, the software and equipment, scheduling and final confirmation responsibilities must be checked per project.

entries: Requirements and collaboration｜Confirm the required sound with the producer and performers.｜Hand over the clarified requirements and the items to clarify, and do not substitute your own opinion for the production's.

Equipment and preparation｜Select and prepare microphones and recording equipment and carry out the checks the task requires.｜Hand over equipment status and issue records; actual operation requires training.
Recording and logs｜Record voices, music and sound effects and keep records.｜Hand over the material and recording logs, keeping original files separate from post-production versions.
Mixing and editing｜Separate and combine sounds and edit productions.｜Hand over revised files and the basis; a paper format check does not replace auditioning.

Synchronization and formats｜Synchronize sound with picture and convert, edit and archive formats.｜Hand over the synchronization notes and files, with parameters checked per actual project requirements.
Issues and handover｜Report equipment anomalies and keep recording logs.｜Hand over the issue recipients and the current status; delivering files does not mean they may be published.

values: S1–S4｜Fictional paper sound documents

No audio is provided, and downloading software, auditioning, wiring, powering up equipment or on-site operation is not required. The parameters and times are project exercise conditions only, not general technical standards, industry safety thresholds or publication permission.

S1｜Delivery requirement R2: project Q requires the two files voice_v2.wav and mix_v3.wav, both 48kHz, 24bit; voice is 1 channel and mix is 2 channels; both require 120 seconds. There is no confirmation allowing other versions or formats.

S2｜Current file table: voice_v2.wav is 48kHz/24bit/1 channel, 120 seconds; mix_v2.wav is 48kHz/24bit/2 channels, 120 seconds; mix_v3.wav is 44.1kHz/24bit/2 channels, 120 seconds. The file table contains no audition result.

S3｜The delivery note says the two files fully comply with R2 and may be published, attaching voice_v2.wav and mix_v3.wav, without attached format revision evidence, producer publication confirmation or material use confirmation. The exercise role checks documents only: technical lead A receives format issues and producer B receives pending publication.

S4｜The same version's picture marks event 01 at 30.000 seconds and event 02 at 90.000 seconds; the sound marks are 30.080 seconds and 89.920 seconds. The fictional record rule is sound time minus picture time, with an absolute difference of no more than 0.050 seconds to meet the paper conditions; whole-film synchronization or sound quality cannot be judged from two points.
Tasks and delivery
List file by file per S1/S2 whether the version, sample rate, bit depth, channels and duration match; find out why the mix cannot use v2 instead of v3.
Calculate the signed and absolute differences per S4 and check the basis for the S3 statement; list pending items, evidence and recipients, seal the first draft, then read the answer.
Reference answer｜Answer independently first

All five voice_v2 items match the paper R2; mix_v2 matches in format and duration but its version is not the required v3; mix_v3 matches in version, bit depth, channels and duration but its 44.1kHz is not 48kHz. There is no fully compliant mix, and this cannot be judged by name alone or by the same 120 seconds.

S4 event 01 difference 30.080−30.000=+0.080 seconds, meaning the sound mark is 80 milliseconds late; event 02 difference 89.920−90.000=−0.080 seconds, meaning 80 milliseconds early. The absolute differences are both 0.080>0.050, so neither point meets the exercise conditions, and a mean difference of zero does not mean the two points are aligned.

The S3 statement that it fully complies with R2 and may be published has no sufficient basis: the mix_v3 sample rate does not match, the S4 two points do not meet the paper conditions, and the audition, material use and publication confirmations are all absent. Pass the format and synchronization pending items to A and the publication and material confirmation issues to B. Mark it pending on paper only, and do not fabricate revisions, automatic conversion, audition conclusions or publication approval.

Matching paper parameters do not equal perceived sound, lawful use, real synchronization or equipment safety; this page does not require listening at high volume, wiring or power testing, or operating a live desk. Real format revisions, audition, synchronization and publication go to personnel with actual training and authorization, and the 0.050 second exercise threshold must not be applied to real projects.

entries.answer: Sound engineering technicians set up and operate sound equipment to record, synchronize, mix, edit or reproduce music, voices and sound effects for stage, film, television, podcast and sports productions. They deliver sound files, recording logs and equipment anomaly records; whether the position leans towards live or post-production work, the software and equipment, scheduling and final confirmation responsibilities must be checked per project.
entries.question: What do sound engineering technicians do?

entries.answer: This occupation centres on sound recording, synchronization, mixing and editing; audio-visual technology leans towards broader event equipment, and broadcast technology also handles signal transmission. Collaboration does not mean the objects, skills and authority are all mutually recognized.

subject.name: Sound engineering technicians
subject.summary: Sound engineering technicians set up and operate sound equipment to record, synchronize, mix, edit or reproduce music, voices and sound effects for stage, film, television, podcast and sports productions. They deliver sound files, recording logs and equipment anomaly records; whether the position leans towards live or post-production work, the software and equipment, scheduling and final confirmation responsibilities must be checked per project.
